newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shippers seek end to cargo charter rules.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shippers seek end to cargo charter rules.

text.p: The Central Bank of Kenya and the Fresh Produce Exporters Association of Kenya (FPEAK) on Friday urged the government and the country's aviation authority to end landing restrictions on chartered cargo flights.

"We are looking for new markets for Kenyan fresh produce but we still see freight problems and air capacity as a bottleneck for development. We need more flexibility for landing rights," said FPEAK Chairman Simon Ethangatta.

"The current problem is that not anyone can land at the airport. You need a special and very strict approval, so even if you can offer a cheaper chartered freight carrier you are not allowed to land," he told Reuters.

Central bank governor Micah Cheserem said he supported the request by the FPEAK to allow private freighters to use chartered cargo flights. He encouraged Kenyan importers to cooperate with horticultural exporters to pool freight costs.

Industry sources said freight costs had dropped over the past few years but inflexibility of landing rights meant they remained high and could take up to 40 percent of the profit from exports of fresh produce.
"With more flexible landing rights you would get more competition between the airlines offering air freight and we could more easily increase exports, and we want to expand," Ethangatta said.
"Horticulture is moving very fast, but a lot of the produce still goes with passenger flights." He urged the authorities to completely remove landing right restrictions for air cargo flights.
He was speaking to delegates at Kenya's annual three-day horticultural exhibition, Hortec '97, which is the biggest such trade fair in sub-Saharan Africa.
Some 90 percent of Kenya's output of flowers, fruits and vegetables is moved by air out of Nairobi, mostly to the Eurpean markets of the Netherlands, Britain, France and Germany.
Europe took 86 percent of the 84,824 tonnes produced in 1996.
Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem told the growers, traders and exporters that he supported the request, recognising horticulture's dependence on air cargo.
"We encourage you to increase areas of cooperation within the industry such as pooling freight so as to reduce costs and expand markets," he said.

"The volume of your exports is now large enough for you to seriously investigate the possibility of cooperation with Kenyan importers so that you could charter planes to export your produce, with Kenyan imports as return cargo," he said.
Speaking to Reuters after the function, Cheserem said there was an obvious need to investigate landing rights.
"The question of freight is very important. The horticulture industry and air cargo industry depend on each other," the central bank governor said.
Ethangatta said anyone who could offer a chartered freighter should be allowed to do so because capacity for fruit and vegetables was a major problem.
"At the moment there is not adequate space available for vegetables and fruits so a lot of that produce has to be transported with passenger planes.

"For flowers it's not a problem, because the destination for flowers is more definite with almost all the flowers going to the Netherlands," he said. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax+5017
